metadata.method: Event identity source-linked with explicit institutional dependence, individual dated claims separately cross-checked, provisional statements never elevated to publish approval.

reviews.title_after: A rain-swollen Beaver Dam Creek breaches Elba's levee during the 1998 Alabama flood
reviews.location_after: Elba and Beaver Dam Creek, Coffee County, Alabama
reviews.second_publisher: U.S. Geological Survey National Water Conditions
reviews.evidence_independence: USGS monthly hydrologic reconstruction versus NCEI storm-data records; both may rely on common rain-gauge and emergency-management reports, but USGS offers independent hydrologic context
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: Heavy rainfall March 6–9, 1998 led Beaver Dam Creek to breach a levee and flood Elba, Alabama; USGS documents more than 9 inches in less than 24 hours in Elba and approximately 2,000 people evacuated.
reviews.unverified_cautions: March 1998 is NOT the separate March 1990 Elba flood. USGS five fatalities refers to the broader Southeast regional storm, not necessarily Elba; verify the exact March 8 breach time and stage crest March 9 before post copy. Do not state all multi-day rain fell March 8.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Elba levee and Beaver Dam Creek watershed map with separate March 6–9 precipitation and March 9 Pea River crest annotations

reviews.title_after: The Good Friday EF4 tornado cuts through Murfreesboro, Tennessee
reviews.location_after: Murfreesboro and Rutherford County, Middle Tennessee
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI Allisona zone report and NWS Nashville detailed assessment share the original tornado damage-survey observations, not two independent wind measurements
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: An EF4 tornado moved through Murfreesboro and other parts of Rutherford County on April 10, 2009 during the Good Friday severe-weather outbreak.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The Allisona NCEI report is a local location segment of the longer EF4, not a separate tornado. Survey-derived ~170 mph peak is not measured 10-m gust, and reported overall outbreak tornado totals must not be substituted for the single Murfreesboro path.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Rutherford County surveyed EF4 track with separate severe-warning timeline and EF rating by surveyed damage location

reviews.title_after: A long-track EF4 tornado devastates Louisville, Mississippi
reviews.location_after: Leake, Attala, Neshoba and Winston Counties, Mississippi
reviews.evidence_independence: The NCEI Zama segment and NWS Jackson event-level path narrative arise from the same operational storm survey; a separate archive web address does not independently measure EF4 winds
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On April 28, 2014, an EF4 tornado tracked through northeast Leake County and across Winston County, inflicting severe damage in Louisville; the NCEI Zama record is an earlier local segment of that track.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Do not count the Zama report and Louisville EF4 as different tornadoes, or assign maximum EF4 damage along the entire path. The April 27–29 multiday outbreak included other tornadoes and casualties, not all attributable to this track.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original county-spanning Louisville EF4 tornado map showing the Zama reporting segment and EF4 locations separately

reviews.title_after: The violent Greenfield EF4 tornado crosses southern Iowa
reviews.location_after: Greenfield and southern Adair County, Iowa
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI Fisk record and NWS Des Moines survey are the same original storm-survey lineage; NWS Omaha's cross-office chronology adds related observations but does not independently rate the EF4
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On May 21, 2024 a violent EF4 tornado tracked through the Greenfield, Iowa area, affecting rural Adams and Adair counties. The NCEI Fisk entry represents an area segment of the larger tornado.
reviews.unverified_cautions: NWS damage-based peak wind estimates of 175–185 mph are not measured gusts, and the page contains historically preliminary line items. Do not treat an EF4 maximum rating as uniform along the track, and distinguish the Greenfield tornado from later Arbor Hill tornado.
reviews.graphic_concept: Rebuild NWS surveyed Greenfield track from agency GIS/KMZ data with EF4 survey sites distinguished from broader circulation and surrounding tornado paths

reviews.title_before: Excessive Heat — GREATER  PORTLAND METRO AREA, Oregon
reviews.title_after: Portland reaches 108°F as the Pacific Northwest heat dome intensifies
reviews.location_after: Portland International Airport and Portland metro, Oregon
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI regional heat narrative and Oregon state emergency review are meteorological versus independent government response accounts; precise airport temperatures originate from the NWS climate station
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: Portland International Airport reached 108°F on June 26, 2021, launching an unprecedented three-day series of record heat; Oregon's state emergency review describes impacts through June 30.
reviews.unverified_cautions: 108°F belongs to June 26; 112°F to June 27 and 116°F to June 28. Do not attribute June 28 all-time station high or full June 25–30 heat mortality to June 26. Distinguish PDX airport readings from neighborhood heat exposure.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original PDX three-day verified station-high step chart (Jun26 108°F, Jun27 112°F, Jun28 116°F) with dated blocking ridge/850-hPa temperature inset

reviews.title_after: The Carr Fire ignites near Whiskeytown Lake before its explosive spread
reviews.location_after: Whiskeytown National Recreation Area, Shasta County, California
reviews.evidence_independence: CAL FIRE's independent incident chronology verifies ignition date, while NCEI documents associated weather conditions; NASA supplies separately acquired satellite observations during later growth
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: The Carr Fire ignited near Whiskeytown Lake in Shasta County on July 23, 2018; California firefighting records mark its start on that date.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The fire's extraordinary spread toward Redding occurred on subsequent days, especially July 26; do not date the large fire-generated vortex or full burned acreage to July 23. Vehicle ignition mechanism should be presented as investigative attribution rather than assumed from satellite data.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original dated progression map from July 23 ignition near Whiskeytown to July 26–27 spread, distinguishing launch-day footprint from eventual perimeter

reviews.title_after: A distant thunderstorm sends a deadly flash flood through Antelope Canyon
reviews.location_after: Antelope Canyon near Page, northern Arizona
reviews.second_publisher: U.S. Geological Survey National Water Conditions
reviews.evidence_independence: USGS national hydrologic monthly account and NCEI original storm data are separate agency archives but their fatality accounting likely comes from the same local incident reports
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: A flash flood struck a narrow slot canyon near Page, Arizona on August 12, 1997. A USGS monthly report documents 11 people killed.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Heavy monsoonal rain fell upstream, not necessarily directly over the hikers. Reconstructed 10–30-foot flood wall figures are retrospective, not direct water-stage instruments at the accident location. Distinguish the Antelope Canyon event from Havasupai flooding two days earlier.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original narrow-canyon watershed and thunderstorm-upstream schematic with source-marked drainage and exact Aug12 timeline

reviews.title_after: Overnight deluges ignite catastrophic flash flooding near Lewiston, Minnesota
reviews.location_after: Lewiston, Stockton and Winona County, southeastern Minnesota
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI Lewiston county report and NWS La Crosse event log share original warning/spotter records; independent daily cooperative snowfall/rainfall records can separately quantify rain when sourced
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: Historic intense rain began the evening of August 18, 2007, leading to deadly flash flooding overnight into August 19 in parts of southeastern Minnesota, including the Lewiston/Stockton corridor.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Do not describe all August 18–20 regional floods as occurring only on August 18. Reported storm-total rainfall and fatalities have broader spatial/time denominators; Hokah 15.10-inch official 24-hour total covers Aug18 8 AM to Aug19 8 AM.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original August 18 evening to August 19 morning radar/rain-gauge time-bar and washout locations, with distinct community fatality scopes

reviews.title_after: Helene's extreme rainfall overwhelms the Nolichucky River near Erwin
reviews.location_after: Erwin, Nolichucky River and northeast Tennessee Appalachians
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI Unicoi County flood report and NWS Morristown regional event review share some storm reports and gauge readings; USGS river station measurements can supply a separate hydrologic observation layer later
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: Hurricane Helene's remnants produced catastrophic river and flash flooding in northeast Tennessee, including the Nolichucky River near Erwin, on September 27, 2024.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Helene's Florida hurricane landfall occurred September 26 EDT, not September 27; rainfall accumulated across multiple days and specific river crest and structural damage timestamps need independent gauges. Avoid counting all Appalachian fatalities as Erwin fatalities.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original September 25–28 Tennessee basin rainfall and Nolichucky river hydrograph timeline, with separate Helene center and local rainfall clocks

reviews.title_before: Blizzard — NORTHERN BLACK HILLS, South Dakota
reviews.title_after: An early-season Black Hills blizzard begins as rain turns toward heavy snow
reviews.location_after: Black Hills and western South Dakota
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI northern Black Hills zone record and NWS Rapid City storm chronology share the regional official reports and surface observations, not distinct meteorological instruments
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: A severe early-season winter storm developed across western South Dakota on October 3, 2013, with the heaviest blizzard conditions spanning October 4–5.
reviews.unverified_cautions: October 3 is the storm onset; extreme snowfall totals and livestock losses largely reflect October 4–5 and broader 3-day period. Storm naming (Atlas, Cattlemen's Blizzard) varies. Never attach peak Friday–Saturday snowfall to Thursday alone.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original October 3–5 snow/rain transition and mountain-wave/blizzard chronology chart with time-zoned NWS surface analyses

reviews.title_before: Dense Fog — ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST, Louisiana
reviews.title_after: Smoke and fog combine into deadly superfog on Louisiana's Interstate 55
reviews.location_after: Interstate 55 Manchac bridge, St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana
reviews.second_publisher: NWS New Orleans/Baton Rouge meteorological StoryMap
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI St. John dense-fog entry and NWS LIX atmospheric reconstruction are within the same NWS/NOAA family; later sheriff incident reporting independently records crash-response scope, but shares state-police vehicle census
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On October 23, 2023, smoke from smoldering marsh fires combined with dense fog and produced extremely low visibility near Interstate 55 at Manchac, Louisiana, contributing to extensive vehicle crashes.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Early NCEI reporting lists 158 vehicles; St. John Sheriff retrospective reports 168 vehicles, 63 injuries and eight fatalities. Final counts and revised casualty investigations must be reconciled with Louisiana State Police; do not publish 158 as final or assume weather was the sole crash cause. No on-road calibrated visibility trace validated.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original hydrometeorological smoke-fog setup chart with time-stamped GOES imagery, LIX sounding inversion, and road corridor; no unlicensed wreck photos

reviews.title_before: Lake-Effect Snow — NORTHERN ERIE, New York
reviews.title_after: A lake-effect snow band begins burying Buffalo's Southtowns
reviews.location_after: Lake Erie snowbelt south and east of Buffalo, western New York
reviews.evidence_independence: The NCEI northern Erie zone narrative and NWS Buffalo retrospective draw from the same official snowfall/spotter observations; no independent sensor is implied solely by the second URL
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: An extraordinary Lake Erie lake-effect event began November 17, 2014 and continued through November 19, dropping several feet of snow in localized parts of the Buffalo Southtowns.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The 5+ foot event accumulation spans November 17–19; do not attribute total to November 17 alone. A second major lake-effect burst followed November 19–21 and must be distinguished from the first storm. Snow reports vary over extremely short distances.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original November 17–19 hourly multi-band lake-effect snow footprint and snowfall-gradient transect, separating first and second storm periods

reviews.title_before: Wildfire — BOULDER & JEFFERSON COUNTIES BELOW 6000 FEET / W BROOMFIELD COUNTY, Colorado
reviews.title_after: Mountain-wave winds fuel the catastrophic Marshall Fire near Boulder
reviews.location_after: Marshall, Superior and Louisville, Boulder County, Colorado
reviews.evidence_independence: NCEI Boulder County wildfire/weather account and NWS Boulder wind assessment share surface observations; NASA Earth Observatory satellite plume imagery is independently observed evidence of timing/extent, not of fire ignition cause
reviews.corroborated_core_claim: On December 30, 2021, intense mountain-wave winds fanned the Marshall Fire from the western Boulder foothills toward Superior and Louisville, Colorado.
reviews.unverified_cautions: NWS documents a localized 115 mph peak gust near Highway 93/72 around noon; it is NOT an on-fire-front 10-m sustained wind or proof of ignition cause. NWS damage counts were time-specific and may differ from final investigations. Distinguish wind-driven spread from separate origin investigation.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original mountain-wave cross-section and dated 11 AM/12 PM/2 PM wind plots over eventual fire perimeter, with independent satellite imagery timing
